catalog_quote: 1.2. STRESS. Stress is marked by increased volume, vowel length, and a slight rise in pitch. Primary stress is highly predictable, occurring on the penultimate syllable in all indigenous forms except for a few two-syllable conjunctions, demonstratives, and pronouns in which primary stress is consistently on the ultimate syllable (e.g. [pa.tíʔ] 'and', [ʔa.tó] 'here', and [ka.ʔáw] 'you').3 Some nonassimilated loan words also have ultimate stress. Secondary stress occurs on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end of the word. It is less intense than primary stress, but is discernible in long words as cadence in which every other vowel is slightly longer and louder than the unstressed vowels in between. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every native word; a closed list of disyllabic conjunctions, demonstratives and pronouns (pati 'and', ato 'here', ka'aw 'you') and some unassimilated Spanish loans take final stress. Secondary stress alternates leftward from the primary (4th and 6th syllables from the end), giving a trochaic cadence in long words. The domain is the phonological word, which includes proclitic and enclitic particles (sec. 1.1, p. 33; orthography note p. 42); a small set of monosyllabic particles (pa 'still', na 'already') carry no stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Secondary stress occurs on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end of the word', i.e. on alternate syllables to the left of the penult; less intense than primary, heard as a cadence in long words, e.g. [ag.pà.malàm.pa.sú.ko] 'I told them to scrub the floor', [kì.na.háŋ.lan] 'need' (p. 34).
new_statements.exceptions: Ultimate stress in a few two-syllable conjunctions, demonstratives and pronouns ([pa.tí] 'and', [ʔa.tó] 'here', [ka.ʔáw] 'you') and in some non-assimilated loanwords; footnote 3 (p. 34): the 1sg pronoun /ʔá.ku/ 'I' takes either ultimate or penultimate stress depending on phrase-level intonation, e.g. [ʔá.ko..] vs [.. a.kó..]; 'Similar stress variation has not been noted with other pronouns.' Monosyllabic particles [pa] 'still', [na] 'already' carry no stress. The Spanish-loan subsystem is treated separately: loans keep their own (sometimes final) stress; vowel allophony rules (sec. 4.4.2, p. 39) are keyed to the 'stressed syllable (usually penultimate)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'A phonological word consists of one or more syllables, with word juncture marked by the stress pattern' (sec. 1.1, p. 33); pre- and postclitic particles count as part of the phonological word for stress and vowel-variant purposes (p. 42). Data collected April-November 1979 on Capul Island, Northern Samar (fn. 1, p. 32). The stress claims are impressionistic (SIL tagmemic phonemic statement), not instrumental.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language 'Sama Abaknon'; fn. 1 (p. 32) says native speakers call it Inabaknon and Samar residents call it Capuleño, and that 'Abaknon' is properly the ethnonym ('one who comes from Abak', the pre-Spanish name of Capul Island). Data were collected on Capul Island, Northern Samar, in 1979 from three named native speakers; no dialect split is described. This is the same languoid as Glottolog inab1237 (ISO abx), no separate dialect glottocode needed.
